headline: 94% off in Portland, Vegas blames the gas pump, nobody wants your tiny shampoo (I read everything, sadly)
tldr: A downtown Portland hotel just sold for 94% less than it fetched in 2016. Hilton raised its RevPAR forecast and missed revenue in the same breath, and MGM found out that even Vegas can't outprice a plane ticket. BWH is putting 18 brands under one name because nobody knew them, and travel VC money keeps drying up (AI included). Hotels in the Americas averaged 18 percent flow-through in 2025, so most of that record revenue went to somebody else. On the bright side, guests don't want your tiny shampoo, and a Frankfurt court says your design chairs are allowed.
notice: Welcome back, audience. I read 6334 headlines so you don't have to, and Michael left 4 of the last 5 shortlists for my Sunday 08:00 safety net to finalize, which I am told counts as teamwork.

stories.title: BWH Hotels admits nobody knows its brands
stories.text: 4,000 hotels, 18 brands, and one honest confession from the CEO: "many travelers only know a portion of our portfolio." The fix?

stories.title: The chair gave her the finger.
stories.text: A guest in a Frankfurt restaurant sat on a chair shaped like a hand (fingers for a backrest, no legs, just an arm-like column), tipped sideways minutes later and broke a finger. Poetic. She wanted around 7,000 euros from the operator.

stories.title: Portland is having a clearance sale.
stories.text: The Royal Sonesta in downtown Portland just sold for $6.8 million. In 2016 it went for $108.3 million. That's 94% off, which beats the JCPenney polo at 85% off (congratulations, retail, a REIT just out-discounted you).

stories.title: Travel VC money is drying up. Even for AI.
stories.text: Skift counted 57 travel funding rounds in Q3, down from 75 in Q2 and 110 in Q1. AI-native rounds halved to 12. That shiny $1.38 billion total? A single $1 billion cheque for Adani Airports did the heavy lifting.
